nodes.label: Edward Said
nodes.date_label: Orientalism 1978 · The Question of Palestine 1979 · Covering Islam 1981 · “Orientalism Reconsidered” 1985 · Culture and Imperialism 1993
nodes.description: A Palestinian-American literary critic whose Orientalism (1978) reads European writing on 'the Orient' as 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient': a discourse in Foucault's sense, durable through what Gramsci called hegemony, though he held, 'unlike Michel Foucault', to 'the determining imprint of individual writers' and denied that the Orient was 'a creation with no corresponding reality'. The Question of Palestine (1979) examined 'Zionism from the Standpoint of Its Victims', Covering Islam (1981) took up American reporting on Islam, and 'Orientalism Reconsidered' (1985) traced Orientalism to historicism, including the 'science of world history'. Culture and Imperialism (1993) added what Orientalism had 'left out', resistance to empire, and proposed reading the metropolitan canon 'contrapuntally, with a simultaneous awareness both of the metropolitan history that is narrated and of those other histories against which (and together with which) the dominating discourse acts'. In period, Bernard Lewis charged him with 'very arbitrary decisions' of scope, and Said replied in their 1982 exchange that it was 'idiotic to say that Orientalism is a conspiracy'; Sadik al-'Azm called his account of Marx 'a travesty' (1981); and a 1996 review summarised feminist critics as holding that critics of Orientalism 'continue to write out gender'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Edward W. Said (1935–2003); Orientalism (1978); The Question of Palestine (1979); Covering Islam (1981); “Orientalism Reconsidered” (Cultural Critique, 1985); foreword to Selected Subaltern Studies (1988); Culture and Imperialism (1993). Readings: Sadik Jalal al-'Azm, “Orientalism and Orientalism in Reverse” (1981); Bernard Lewis, “The Question of Orientalism” and the Said–Lewis exchange (New York Review of Books, 1982); Cheryl McEwan on Reina Lewis, Gendering Orientalism (1996). Later: Robert Irwin, Dangerous Knowledge (2006).
nodes.scope_note: A literary critic, not a historian; the entry is for a framework historians meet across fields. It rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: Orientalism in the 1978 Pantheon first edition (introduction pp. 1–28 in full; pp. 94, 153–156, 204 and 321 for passages used); The Question of Palestine (1980 Vintage reprint of the 1979 book; pp. 56–59 and 74–76); the Covering Islam introduction (p. ix); 'Orientalism Reconsidered' (1985) in full; the foreword to Selected Subaltern Studies (1988, pp. v–x) in full; and Culture and Imperialism (1993 Knopf first edition; introduction pp. xii–xiv and xxv, and pp. 41–42, 51, 66, 240–245, 251 and 278). Not read: 'Traveling Theory' (The World, the Text, and the Critic, 1983) and 'Foucault and the Imagination of Power' (1986), both lending-only or closed here; his critique of Foucault is taken from Culture and Imperialism, which cites the 1986 essay as 'my critique'. He is not presented as a founder: a 1992 critique calls his blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' (O'Hanlon and Washbrook, first page only) and a 1996 review calls Orientalism 'undoubtedly' the inspiration behind critical interest in 'empire, knowledge and power' (McEwan); these are readers' judgements. Contested in period by Lewis (1982) and al-'Azm (1981), both read; James Clifford's review (History and Theory, 1980), Lata Mani and Ruth Frankenberg (Economy and Society, 1985), Dennis Porter (1983) and Aijaz Ahmad (1991–92) are recorded but were not read: Porter is known here from Said's 1985 reply, Ahmad from Robert Irwin's later account (2006), Reina Lewis (1996) from McEwan's review. No post-2000 work by Said is used; Irwin (2006) is a labelled later reading.

nodes.label: Ranajit Guha
nodes.date_label: A Rule of Property for Bengal 1963 · “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” 1982 · Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency 1983 · “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency” 1983 · “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography” 1989 (book 1997)
nodes.description: A historian of colonial India, who taught at Sussex and the Australian National University and edited Subaltern Studies from its first volume (1982) until he left the editorial team in 1988. The opening statement holds that the historiography of Indian nationalism 'has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism', and that it leaves out 'the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain' that 'neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', while allowing 'a great deal of overlap' between the two (1982). Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983) attributes 'a consciousness' to the rebel peasant, holds that Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India', and reads that consciousness through the records of counter-insurgency; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (1983) finds colonial, nationalist and radical histories alike making the rebel 'only a contingent element in another history with another subject'. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989; book 1997) defines hegemony, against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony', as dominance in which 'Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)', and argues that colonial dominance had 'quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony'. In period, Spivak (1985) read the recovery of subaltern consciousness as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', O'Hanlon (1988) found 'the classic figure of Western humanism' readmitted 'in the figure of the subaltern himself', Bayly (1988) found that the approach sometimes seemed to postulate an 'unchanging peasantry', and Sarkar (1997) an 'unnoticed drift' towards nationalist positions 'even in Guha's initial formulation of the project'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Ranajit Guha (1923–2023); A Rule of Property for Bengal: An Essay on the Idea of Permanent Settlement (Paris: Mouton, 1963); Preface and “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India”, Subaltern Studies I (1982); Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (Delhi, 1983); “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency”, Subaltern Studies II (1983); “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography”, Subaltern Studies VI (1989), and Dominance without Hegemony: History and Power in Colonial India (1997); Selected Subaltern Studies, edited with Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (1988). Readings: Spivak (1985); O'Hanlon (1988); Bayly (1988); Sarkar (1997); Chakrabarty (2000).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the Subaltern Studies I preface and opening statement in the Selected Subaltern Studies reprint (1988, pp. 35–44); the introduction of Elementary Aspects (pp. 1–17), its bibliography and pp. 89–90; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983, pp. 1–42) in full; and 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (Subaltern Studies VI, 1989), pp. 210–215, 227–233, 276–277, 291–292 and 299–303. The 1963 and 1997 books are known here only from metadata and from later quotation; the rest of Elementary Aspects and of the 1989 essay is unread. He is not presented as the founder of a field. In period, Chakrabarty called him 'the founder of the group' (1997) and James C. Scott wrote that Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document' of 'the Subaltern Studies School', while finding 'school' too rigid a term (1999); his own 1982 statement claims 'no more than to try and indicate an orientation'. Contested in period by Spivak (1985, a reading from within the project), O'Hanlon (1988), Bayly (1988) and Sarkar (1997); Javeed Alam's Marxist critique (Social Scientist, 1983) is known only through O'Hanlon and is unread. Vinay Bahl (1997) is unread. Chakrabarty's 2000 account of the project is a member's later reading and carries no edge alone. Not Ramachandra Guha, the environmental historian, who has a separate people record.

nodes.label: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
nodes.date_label: Of Grammatology (translation) 1976 · “Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography” 1985 · “Three Women’s Texts” 1985 · “Can the Subaltern Speak?” 1988 · A Critique of Postcolonial Reason 1999
nodes.description: A literary theorist and the translator of Derrida’s Of Grammatology (1976), whose essays on colonial India became reference points for historians. In ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’ (1985) she read the collective ‘from within but against the grain’, proposing that its recovery of subaltern consciousness be read ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’, and argued that it overlooked ‘how important the concept-metaphor woman is’ to its own discourse. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988) separates representation as ‘speaking for’ from ‘re-presentation’, argues that in Foucault and Deleuze’s conversation intellectuals, ‘representing them, ... represent themselves as transparent’, and reads the British abolition of sati through the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, set against the nativist ‘The women actually wanted to die’: between them ‘One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness.’ She later called the essay’s closing ‘the subaltern cannot speak!’ ‘an inadvisable remark’ (1999). In period, Gyan Prakash (1992) held that she ‘very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman’ as a limit of historical understanding, Rosalind O’Hanlon (1988) urged hesitation ‘before accepting’ her proposal to re-inscribe the series’ strategy ‘as a strategy for our times’, and Terry Eagleton (1999), crediting the book with addressing ‘the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’, found her Critique ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ and ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (b. 1942); translator’s preface to Jacques Derrida, Of Grammatology (1976); “Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography” (Subaltern Studies IV, 1985; introduction to Selected Subaltern Studies, 1988); “Three Women’s Texts and a Critique of Imperialism” (Critical Inquiry, 1985); “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (in Nelson and Grossberg, eds., Marxism and the Interpretation of Culture, 1988; revised in A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, 1999); “The New Subaltern: A Silent Interview” (2000). Readings: O’Hanlon (1988); Chakrabarty (1992); Prakash (1992); Sarkar (1994); Pandey (1995); Eagleton (1999); Chatterjee (2010).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ in the 1988 text as reprinted in Williams and Chrisman, Colonial Discourse and Post-Colonial Theory (1993; pp. 66–111, opening abridged), with page numbers of that reprint; two 1988 page anchors (p. 277 and p. 308) come from Chakrabarty (1992, n. 48) and Sunder Rajan (2010). The 1999 revision was read in Morris’s 2010 reprint, which has no page numbers. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’ was read in Subaltern Studies IV (1985), pp. 330–363, in full; ‘Three Women’s Texts’ pp. 243–245; the translator’s preface to Of Grammatology at p. lxxvii of the 1997 corrected edition. She is a literary critic, not a historian, and is not presented as a founder of postcolonial studies; she joined the Subaltern Studies editorial collective in the 1990s (Chaturvedi gives Subaltern Studies IX, 1996; Chatterjee recalls 1993) and in 2000 called herself ‘a sometime member’. Benita Parry’s in-period critique (Oxford Literary Review, 1987), Aijaz Ahmad’s In Theory (1992) and Lata Mani’s work on sati (1987, 1998) were not read; Ahmad appears only through Eagleton’s report of her contrast with him. Chatterjee (2010) is a later reading by a member of the collective and carries no in-period claim.

edges.relationship: Orientalism as discourse and as a style of domination: Western knowledge and representation of 'the Orient' read through knowledge and power, extended to contrapuntal reading of the metropolitan canon with empire (1978–93)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Orientalism (New York: Pantheon, 1978, first edition; page images checked): 'The Orient was almost a European invention' (p. 1); Orientalism as 'a style of thought based upon an ontological and epistemological distinction made between "the Orient" and (most of the time) "the Occident"' (p. 2) and as 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient' (p. 3). He qualifies it at once: 'it would be wrong to conclude that the Orient was essentially an idea, or a creation with no corresponding reality'; 'The relationship between Occident and Orient is a relationship of power, of domination, of varying degrees of a complex hegemony' (p. 5); and he leaves open 'how one can study other cultures and peoples from a libertarian, or a nonrepressive and nonmanipulative, perspective. But then one would have to rethink the whole complex problem of knowledge and power' (p. 24). Covering Islam (1981, introduction, p. ix): 'The underlying theme of Orientalism is the affiliation of knowledge with power.' 'Orientalism Reconsidered', Cultural Critique 1 (1985), read in full: the issues are 'the representation of other cultures, societies, histories; the relationship between power and knowledge' (p. 89); 'what for the most part got left out of Orientalism was precisely the very history that resisted its ideological as well as political encroachments' (p. 94); 'Orientalism is a praxis of the same sort, albeit in different territories, as male gender dominance, or patriarchy' (p. 103). Culture and Imperialism (New York: Knopf, 1993, first edition): 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii); 'we begin to reread it not univocally but contrapuntally, with a simultaneous awareness both of the metropolitan history that is narrated and of those other histories against which (and together with which) the dominating discourse acts' (p. 51); 'contrapuntal reading must take account of both processes, that of imperialism and that of resistance to it' (p. 66). In-period reception and criticism. Bernard Lewis, 'The Question of Orientalism', New York Review of Books, 24 June 1982 (web text, read in full, no page numbers): 'To prove this point, Mr. Said makes a number of very arbitrary decisions. His Orient is reduced to the Middle East, and his Middle East to a part of the Arab world'; 'a history of Arabic studies in Europe without the Germans makes as much sense as would a history of European music or philosophy with the same omission'; 'The most rigorous and penetrating critique of Orientalist scholarship has always been and will remain that of the Orientalists themselves.' Said's reply (NYRB, 12 August 1982): 'It is idiotic to say that Orientalism is a conspiracy or to suggest that "the West" is evil', while its 'modern discourse is correctly perceived as a discourse of power'; Lewis answered that 'It is difficult to argue with a scream of rage' and that the book 'takes a genuine problem of real importance, and reduces it to the level of political polemic and personal abuse'. Sadik Jalal al-'Azm, 'Orientalism and Orientalism in Reverse', Khamsin 8 (1981) (web text, read in full) credits 'laying bare Orientalism's persistent belief that there exists a radical ontological difference' between Orient and Occident, but holds that tracing Orientalism back to Homer 'simply lends strength to the essentialistic categories of "Orient" and "Occident"'. Rosalind O'Hanlon and David Washbrook (CSSH 1992; first-page extract only, as recorded in its source note) call Said's blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' in Indian colonial history. Cheryl McEwan, Journal of Historical Geography 22 (1996), read in full: 'The inspiration behind the critical interest in empire, knowledge and power was undoubtedly Edward Said's groundbreaking and provocative Orientalism' (p. 489); feminist scholars 'argue that the critics of Orientalism and ethnocentric scholarship continue to write out gender' (p. 489); Reina Lewis's Gendering Orientalism (1996) is 'a response to Said in its efforts to destabilize the homogenizing tendencies of twentieth-century critiques of Orientalism' (p. 490). Said answered Dennis Porter's charge that he is 'ahistorical and inconsistent' as 'more weighty in assertion than it is in proof' (1985, p. 90); Porter's essay (1983) was not read. Not read: James Clifford's review essay (History and Theory 19, 1980) and Lata Mani and Ruth Frankenberg, 'The Challenge of Orientalism' (Economy and Society 14, 1985); both are recorded as metadata only. Later reading, labelled: Robert Irwin (2006, p. 299) writes that 'Early reviews of Orientalism were mostly hostile'. A contribution to postcolonial critique; the evidence does not make him its founder. edge_107 (language → post), edge_419 (post → indigenous) and edge_693 (post → geography) name him as a resource for others and stay.

edges.relationship: Foucault's notion of discourse used to identify Orientalism, with an explicit disagreement over the weight of individual authors (1978)
edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978; page images checked): 'I have found it useful here to employ Michel Foucault's notion of a discourse, as described by him in The Archaeology of Knowledge and in Discipline and Punish, to identify Orientalism. My contention is that without examining Orientalism as a discourse one cannot possibly understand the enormously systematic discipline by which European culture was able to manage—and even produce—the Orient politically, sociologically, militarily, ideologically, scientifically, and imaginatively during the post-Enlightenment period' (p. 3). 'Yet unlike Michel Foucault, to whose work I am greatly indebted, I do believe in the determining imprint of individual writers upon the otherwise anonymous collective body of texts constituting a discursive formation like Orientalism'; 'Foucault believes that in general the individual text or author counts for very little; empirically, in the case of Orientalism (and perhaps nowhere else) I find this not to be so' (p. 23). Elsewhere he writes of 'what Michel Foucault calls a discourse, whose material presence or weight, not the originality of a given author, is really responsible for the texts produced out of it' (p. 94), and he groups 'Gramsci, certainly, and Foucault and Raymond Williams in their very different ways' as illustrating that hegemonic culture's constraints on writers 'were productive, not unilaterally inhibiting' (p. 14). In-period criticism of the combination: al-'Azm (1981, read) objects that for Said 'representations, images, words, metaphors ... are, if not the very stuff of reality, then certainly much more important and informative substitutes for raw reality itself'. Later reading, labelled: Irwin (2006, pp. 289–290) sets the p. 23 and p. 94 passages against each other and argues that 'Foucault and Gramsci have different and contrasting notions of discourse'; Ahmad (1991–92) is reported by Irwin (p. 300) as finding that 'Said's allegiance to Foucault ... got him into the worst muddles'; Ahmad's texts were not read. The edge records Said's stated use and revision of Foucault, not a reading of Foucault's own position; Said's later criticism is edge 4.

edges.relationship: Gramsci's hegemony and civil society used to explain the durability of Orientalism, and his 'inventory' of historical traces taken as the book's personal starting point (1978); consent for distant rule framed as 'a very Gramscian' question (1993)
edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978; page images checked): 'Gramsci has made the useful analytic distinction between civil and political society'; culture works in civil society 'not through domination but by what Gramsci calls consent'; 'the form of this cultural leadership is what Gramsci has identified as hegemony, an indispensable concept for any understanding of cultural life in the industrial West. It is hegemony, or rather the result of cultural hegemony at work, that gives Orientalism the durability and the strength I have been speaking about so far' (pp. 6–7). Orientalism depends on 'this flexible positional superiority, which puts the Westerner in a whole series of possible relationships with the Orient without ever losing him the relative upper hand' (p. 7). 'In the Prison Notebooks Gramsci says: "The starting-point of critical elaboration is the consciousness of what one really is ..."'; Said notes that the English translation omits Gramsci's conclusion, 'therefore it is imperative at the outset to compile such an inventory', and calls his study 'an attempt to inventory the traces upon me, the Oriental subject' (p. 25). Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993): 'The important point—a very Gramscian one—is how the national British, French, and American cultures maintained hegemony over the peripheries. How within them was consent gained and continuously consolidated for the distant rule of native peoples and territories?' (p. 51). In 1988 he described the Subaltern Studies scholars as influenced by 'many varieties of Western Marxism, Gramsci's most eminently' (foreword, Selected Subaltern Studies, p. x). Later reading, labelled: Irwin (2006, pp. 289–290) argues that 'Foucault and Gramsci had rather different ideas about the relationship between power and knowledge'. The edge records Said's stated use of Gramsci; it makes no claim about Gramsci's own Orient, which Said does not discuss in the pages read.

edges.relationship: Foucault criticised for discounting individual authors (1978) and for ignoring empire and dissolving the individual in a 'microphysics of power' that it is 'hopeless to resist' (1993)
edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (1978): 'Foucault believes that in general the individual text or author counts for very little; empirically, in the case of Orientalism (and perhaps nowhere else) I find this not to be so' (p. 23), while declaring himself 'greatly indebted' to Foucault (p. 23). Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993): of Foucault and Raymond Williams, 'In the main I am in considerable sympathy with the genealogical discoveries of these two formidable scholars, and greatly indebted to them. Yet for both the imperial experience is quite irrelevant, a theoretical oversight that is the norm in Western cultural and scientific disciplines' (p. 41). Comparing Foucault and Fanon: 'Foucault's work moves further and further away from serious consideration of social wholes, focussing instead upon the individual as dissolved in an ineluctably advancing "microphysics of power" that it is hopeless to resist'; 'ignoring the imperial context of his own theories, Foucault seems actually to represent an irresistible colonizing movement that paradoxically fortifies the prestige of both the lonely individual scholar and the system that contains him'; Foucault 'swerves away from politics entirely' (p. 278). His note 198 refers the reader to 'my critique in "Foucault and the Imagination of Power"' (in David Hoy, ed., Foucault: A Critical Reader, 1986, pp. 149–155); that essay, and 'Traveling Theory' (1983), were not read. On p. 26 he also describes Foucault's turn to 'the local micro-physics of power that surround the individual'. Foucault's position is given only as Said presents it; no reply by Foucault was looked for. The critique is from a writer who kept using Foucault (edge 2); it is a disagreement within an acknowledged debt. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) records other postcolonial critics' engagements and stays.

edges.relationship: Marx's 1853 writings on British rule in India read as an instance in which Orientalist generalisation overrode his sympathy for Asian suffering (1978), a reading contested in period as a travesty
edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978; page images checked), pp. 153–156. Marx 'identified the notion of an Asiatic economic system in his 1853 analyses of British rule in India, and then put beside that immediately the human depredation introduced into this system by English colonial interference, rapacity, and outright cruelty' (p. 153). After quoting Marx on England as 'the unconscious tool of history' and his Goethe citation: 'Marx's economic analyses are perfectly fitted thus to a standard Orientalist undertaking, even though Marx's humanity, his sympathy for the misery of people, are clearly engaged. Yet in the end it is the Romantic Orientalist vision that wins out' (p. 154); 'The idea of regenerating a fundamentally lifeless Asia is a piece of pure Romantic Orientalism' (p. 154); 'Marx is no exception. The collective Orient was easier for him to use in illustration of a theory than existential human identities' (p. 155); 'In part, of course, Marx was concerned with vindicating his own theses on socio-economic revolution' (p. 155); Marx is 'the case by which a non-Orientalist's human engagements were first dissolved, then usurped by Orientalist generalizations' (p. 156). The introduction announces it: 'The same kind of paradox is to be found in Marx, as I try to show in this book' (p. 14). In 1985 he names Marx among the historicists whose one human history 'either culminated in or was observed from the vantage point of Europe' ('Orientalism Reconsidered', p. 101). Marx's words appear here only as Said quotes them; the 1853 articles were not read. In-period counter-critique: al-'Azm (Khamsin 1981, read): 'I think that this account of Marx's views and analyses of highly complex historical processes and situations is a travesty'; 'only Said's excessive fascination with the verbal, textual and linguistic could lead him to portray Marx's mind as somehow usurped'; Marx's explanation 'testifies to his theoretical consistency in general, and to his keen realism'. Aijaz Ahmad's criticism of the same pages ('Between Orientalism and Historicism', Studies in History 1991; In Theory, 1992) is known here only from Irwin (2006, n. 32 to p. 296), who reports that Ahmad suggests 'Marx's position on rural Indians was not significantly different from his position on rural Germans'; Ahmad was not read. Later reading, labelled: Irwin (2006, pp. 295–296) calls the treatment a travesty and asks why there is no discussion of 'the Asiatic mode of production, Oriental despotism'.

edges.relationship: The named world-historical syntheses (Braudel, Wallerstein, Perry Anderson, Wolf) criticised as heir to Orientalist historicism: a homogenising scheme observed from a European vantage point that avoids its own relation to imperialism (1985); not a critique of every global or connected-history method
edges.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. 'Orientalism Reconsidered', Cultural Critique 1 (Autumn 1985), pp. 89–107, read in full (JSTOR copy). 'One of the legacies of Orientalism, and indeed one of its epistemological foundations, is historicism'; historicism 'meant that the one human history uniting humanity either culminated in or was observed from the vantage point of Europe, or the West'; out of the recuperation of what 'Eric Wolf has called people without history ... a still later disciplinary step was taken, the founding of the science of world history, whose major practitioners include Braudel, Wallerstein, Perry Anderson, and Wolf himself' (p. 101). He grants it 'greater capacity for dealing with ... the non-synchronous experiences of Europe's Other', but finds 'a fairly uniform avoidance of the relationship between European imperialism and these variously constituted, variously formed and articulated knowledges' (p. 101). 'The curious result is that the theories of accumulation on a world scale, or the capitalist world state, or lineages of absolutism depend (a) on the same displaced percipient and historicist observer who had been an Orientalist or colonial traveler three generations ago; (b) they depend also on a homogenizing and incorporating world historical scheme that assimilated non-synchronous developments, histories, cultures, and peoples to it'; 'the problem is once again historicism' (p. 102). He also rejects 're-cycling the old Marxist or world-historical rhetoric' (p. 103). In 1993 he contrasts revisionist works with 'the so-called world historians as well as the colonial Orientalists, who have tended to herd immense amounts of material under simple and all-encompassing rubrics' (Culture and Imperialism, pp. 41–42). The named historians' positions appear only as Said characterises them; no replies were looked for. The critique names practitioners mapped across several entries (Wolf on global; Wallerstein on dependency; Anderson on historicalsociology; Braudel's person entry); global is the target because he names 'the science of world history' as the object. edge_124 (post → global, Chakrabarty) stays.

edges.relationship: Foreword introducing Subaltern Studies to an Anglo-American readership, with his own caution that subaltern and elite histories are 'different but overlapping and curiously interdependent territories' (1988)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period text. Foreword to Ranajit Guha and Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, eds., Selected Subaltern Studies (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1988), pp. v–x, read in full (page images of a Digital Library of India scan, OCR checked against the images). He describes Guha's opening essay as 'fiercely theoretical and intellectually insurrectionary' (p. v) and the word subaltern as deriving 'from Gramsci's usage in the Prison Notebooks' (p. vi); 'rewriting Indian history today is an extension of the struggle between subaltern and elite' (p. vii). His addition: 'Yet even though his analysis is explicit on all the main issues, there is something that could perhaps be added to it here. And that is that no matter how one tried to extricate subaltern from elite histories, they are different but overlapping and curiously interdependent territories. This, I believe, is a crucial point. For if subaltern history is construed to be only a separatist enterprise ... then it runs the risk of just being a mirror opposite the writing whose tyranny it disputes' (p. viii). He places the group in 'the vast post-colonial cultural and critical effort' (p. ix) and calls its borrowing from Foucault 'the sharing of a paradigm, rather than slavish copying' (p. x); the volume is 'a crossing of boundaries, a smuggling of ideas across lines' (p. x). In 1985 he had already listed 'the group around Ranajit Guha (Subaltern Studies)' among anti-Orientalist projects ('Orientalism Reconsidered', pp. 104–105). A contribution of framing and reception to the series' Anglo-American appearance; it does not make him a member of the collective, a founder, or the source of its theory (the existing roster row says the same). edge_115 (subaltern → post) stays.

edges.relationship: Culture and Imperialism's account of resistance culture: anticolonial histories such as James's The Black Jacobins and Antonius's The Arab Awakening read as a 'voyage in' to metropolitan culture, alongside post-independence critiques by Guha and Alatas (1993)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period text. Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993), chapter 3, 'Resistance and Opposition'. He distinguishes liberal anti-colonialism, which did 'not dispute the fundamental superiority of Western man', from anti-imperialism, and argues 'there was no overall condemnation of imperialism until—and this is my point—after native uprisings were too far gone to be ignored or defeated' (pp. 240–241). Anti-imperialist work by writers from the peripheries in the metropolis is 'usually an extension into the metropolis of large-scale mass movements'; 'There is thus an overlap and interdependence that cannot theoretically be described as only the reactive assertion of a separate colonial or native identity'; 'The voyage in, then, constitutes an especially interesting variety of hybrid cultural work' (p. 244). He reads 'C.L.R. James's The Black Jacobins, published in 1938, and, appearing at almost the same time, George Antonius's The Arab Awakening' as works 'intended as serious works of scholarship and advocacy addressed from within a national movement for independence to a general audience', set against Ranajit Guha's A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963) and S. H. Alatas's The Myth of the Lazy Native (1977), which are 'post-colonial and specialist' (p. 245); 'history for Guha is critique, not the dutiful replication of colonialist objects, ideologies, and arguments' (p. 251). He also treats Fanon as one who 'programmatically seeks to treat colonial and metropolitan societies together' (p. 278). The introduction frames the chapter: 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii). Read: pp. xii, 240–245, 251, 278; the rest of the chapter (including the Fanon and Cabral sections) was not read closely. No in-period review assessing this chapter for historians was read. A contribution to how anticolonial histories are read and placed, not a claim that he wrote anticolonial history in their sense; The Question of Palestine (1979) is mentioned in the node, not used for this edge.

edges.relationship: The programme statement of Subaltern Studies: a critique of colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist elitism, an autonomous but overlapping domain of 'the politics of the people', and a method of reading rebel consciousness through counter-insurgency records (1982–83)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Preface to Subaltern Studies I (dated Canberra, August 1981), read in the Selected Subaltern Studies reprint (Oxford, 1988), p. 35: the series is to 'rectify the elitist bias characteristic of much research and academic work' in South Asian studies; 'subaltern' is taken in the Concise Oxford sense, 'of inferior rank', as 'a name for the general attribute of subordination in South Asian society whether this is expressed in terms of class, caste, age, gender and office or in any other way'. 'On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India' (same reprint, pp. 37–44; Subaltern Studies I pagination is pp. 1–8): elitist historiography 'is of course not without its uses' (p. 38) but 'fails to acknowledge, far less interpret, the contribution made by the people on their own, that is, independently of the elite' (p. 39); 'What clearly is left out of this un-historical historiography is the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain, for it neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', 'As modern as indigenous elite politics' (p. 40); the two domains were not 'hermetically sealed off'; 'there was a great deal of overlap' (p. 42); the same class 'dominant in one area ... could be among the dominated in another' (p. 44). He claims a direction, not a doctrine: 'Let a hundred flowers blossom and we don't mind even the weeds' (p. 43); 'We claim no more than to try and indicate an orientation' (p. 43). Method, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983), introduction read (Duke 1999 printing, which keeps the 1983 Oxford pagination): 'To acknowledge the peasant as the maker of his own rebellion is to attribute ... a consciousness to him' (p. 4); 'How then are we to get in touch with the consciousness of insurgency when our access to it is barred thus by the discourse of counter-insurgency?'; 'It should be possible therefore to read the presence of a rebel consciousness as a necessary and pervasive element within that body of evidence' (p. 15). 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency', Subaltern Studies II (Delhi, 1983), pp. 1–42, read in full: historiography takes the peasant rebel 'merely as an empirical person or member of a class, but not as an entity whose will and reason constituted the praxis called rebellion' (p. 2); 'Cause is made to stand in as a phantom surrogate for Reason' (p. 3); the historian should 'stop pretending that it can fully grasp a past consciousness and reconstitute it' (p. 33). In-period reception, a member's reading first: Spivak, 'Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography', Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363 (read): the group 'offers a theory of change' (p. 330); its practice is 'closer to deconstruction' (p. 332) and its presuppositions are 'not, strictly speaking, consonant with a desire to find a consciousness (here of the subaltern) in a positive and pure state' (p. 333); quoting Elementary Aspects p. 15, she reads 'the project to retrieve the subaltern consciousness' 'as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest' (pp. 341–342), which 'would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness' (p. 356); 'The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women' but overlooks 'how important the concept-metaphor woman is' (p. 356). Rosalind O'Hanlon, 'Recovering the Subject' (Modern Asian Studies 22:1, 1988, pp. 189–224; read in the Verso reprint, 2000, pp. 72–115, whose pages are cited): 'the classic figure of Western humanism—the self-originating, self-determining individual ... is readmitted through the back door in the figure of the subaltern himself' (p. 74). C. A. Bayly, 'Rallying Around the Subaltern' (Journal of Peasant Studies 16:1, 1988, pp. 110–120; Verso reprint pp. 116–126): the Subalterns 'acted mainly as a catalyst' for an existing minority interest (p. 116); Guha's approach 'seems sometimes to postulate the existence of an unchanging peasantry and unified peasant consciousness defined by struggle with colonialism' (p. 121). Sumit Sarkar, 'The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies' (1997; pp. 82–87 and 90–94 read, pp. 84–87 against the page images): the early volumes were 'largely ignored in the West' while debated in 'Left-leaning intellectual circles in India' (p. 84); 'it was argued with considerable justice by Guha and other contributors' that anti-colonial movements had been explained 'far too often' by economic pressures and mobilization from the top (p. 85); the claims of a new 'paradigm' 'were certainly over-flamboyant' (p. 86); the theoretical turn 'had its origins in Guha's attempt to use some of the language and methods of Lévi-Straussian structuralism' (p. 87). Founder language is attributed, not adopted: Chakrabarty (1997) calls him 'the founder of the group' (subaltern source); Scott's foreword to the 1999 Duke printing writes that Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document of what is now known as the Subaltern Studies School', adding that 'The term school conveys far too much in the way of a rigid orthodoxy' (p. ix). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (Nepantla, 2000) treats 'the work of the historian Ranajit Guha in the period when he acted as the founding editor' as 'the founding texts of the project' (p. 11). edge_115 (subaltern → post) and edge_159 (gramsci → subaltern) stay.

edges.relationship: Colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist histories of India criticised as two forms of elitism that write nationalism as 'a sort of spiritual biography of the Indian elite' and leave out popular initiative (1982), extended to the shared liberal assumption that colonial dominance was hegemonic (1989)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. 'On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India' (1982; Selected Subaltern Studies reprint, 1988, pp. 37–44, read): 'The historiography of Indian nationalism has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism'; both 'share the prejudice that the making of the Indian nation and the development of the consciousness—nationalism—which informed this process were exclusively or predominantly elite achievements' (p. 37). The colonialist kind treats nationalism as 'a sort of “learning process”' driven by 'the expectation of rewards' (p. 38); the nationalist kind writes it up 'as a sort of spiritual biography of the Indian elite' (p. 38). Neither can explain 'the anti-Rowlatt upsurge of 1919 and the Quit India movement of 1942' as 'popular initiative asserting itself ... in defiance or absence of elite control' (p. 39). The qualification he keeps: 'Elitist historiography is of course not without its uses' (p. 38), and 'even the elitists have a part to play if only by way of teaching by negative examples' (p. 43). 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983, read): in bourgeois-nationalist historiography 'it is an elite consciousness which is read into all peasant movements as their motive force', producing 'such grotesqueries as the characterization of the Indigo Rebellion of 1860 as “the first non-violent mass movement”' (p. 38). 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (Subaltern Studies VI, 1989, pp. 210–309; pp. 210–215, 227–233, 291–292 and 299–303 read): 'There was one Indian battle that Britain never won. It was a battle for appropriation of the Indian past' (p. 210); 'History became thus a game for two to play as the alien colonialist project of appropriation was matched by an indigenous nationalist project of counter-appropriation' (p. 212); both rest on 'a fundamental agreement between the Indian bourgeoisie and the British' from 'the standpoint of liberalism' (p. 212); 'dominance under colonial conditions has quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony' (p. 228). On the Cambridge historians: 'The subject of this neo-colonialist historiography is the Empire' (p. 292); Anil Seal's 'general explanation' is 'a kind of academic confidence trick' (p. 300). In-period criticism of the stance: Sarkar (1997, p. 92, read) sees 'an unnoticed drift implicit even in Guha's initial formulation of the project in Subaltern Studies I': 'The “historiography of colonial India” somehow slides quickly into that of Indian nationalism', and the central problematic 'ultimately becomes “the historic failure of the nation to come into its own”' (quoting Subaltern Studies I, pp. 2–3, 7). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000, p. 14) describes the series as starting 'as a critique of two contending schools of history: the Cambridge school and that of the nationalist historians'. This edge carries the story now told by edge_604 (subaltern → nationaltradition), whose relabel is proposed; edge_114 (subaltern → anticolonial) is discussed under edge_revisions.

edges.relationship: Peasant insurgency in colonial India read as deliberate political action against a composite dominance of landlord, moneylender and state, whose limits define 'the quality of that politics' rather than denying it (1983)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983), introduction pp. 1–17 read (Duke 1999 printing; 1983 Oxford pagination, checked against the Delhi edition's text): 'Insurgency was thus the necessary antithesis of colonialism' (p. 2); the first histories of revolt were 'a discourse of power' (p. 3). Spontaneity is rejected as 'an idea that is elitist as well as erroneous' (p. 4). For colonial India, 'there was nothing in the militant movements of its rural masses that was not political' (p. 6), because 'the hitherto discrete powers of the landlord, the moneylender and the official came to form, under colonial rule, a composite apparatus of dominance over the peasant', a subjection 'primarily political in character' (p. 8). 'There was nothing spontaneous about all this in the sense of being unthinking and wanting in deliberation'; 'insurgency affirmed its political character precisely by its negative and inversive procedure' (p. 9). He keeps the limits: rebel aims that failed 'to rise above localism, sectarianism and ethnicity' do 'not take away from the essentially political character of their activity but defines the quality of that politics by specifying its limitations' (p. 10); 'It would be wrong of course to overestimate the maturity of this politics' (p. 10); it was 'a somewhat inchoate and naive state of consciousness' (p. 11). In-period criticism: O'Hanlon (1988; Verso reprint, 2000) sets his book apart from cruder 'literal' readings of autonomy ('I want to distinguish Ranajit Guha's work in the book Elementary Aspects', p. 85), yet, following Dipankar Gupta, finds the 'culturological' style 'carried to an extreme' there, so that 'the failure of peasant movements to spread' is explained by a 'habit of thinking and acting on a small and local scale' rather than by structural features (pp. 86–87); she sees 'his forceful insistence upon humanism's unitary subject-agent in its most extreme form' (p. 89). Sarkar (1997) writes that Guha's analyses of rumour, crime and insurgency 'were appreciated by many who could not accept the overall framework of Elementary Aspects' (p. 86). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000) calls the redefinition of 'the political' 'the critical theoretical break' (p. 15). The related critique of Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' is edge 4. edge_357 (subaltern → political) tells the same story under Guha's name; its relabel is proposed.

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm's category 'pre-political', credited as pioneering, judged to help 'little in understanding the experience of colonial India', where peasant militancy was political (1983)
edges.evidence_note: His own text. Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983), introduction pp. 5–6 read (Duke 1999 printing; 1983 Oxford pagination): those who identify consciousness with organization and politics can call mass activity 'unconscious, hence pre-political' (p. 5). 'The image of the pre-political peasant rebel in societies still to be fully industrialized owes a great deal to E. J. Hobsbawm's pioneering work published over two decades ago'; Hobsbawm 'uses this term again and again to describe a state of supposedly absolute or near absence of political consciousness or organization' (p. 5). Hobsbawm's words as Guha quotes them: 'the social brigand appears ... only before the poor have reached political consciousness or acquired more effective methods of social agitation'; 'The bandit is a pre-political phenomenon and his strength is in inverse proportion to that of organized revolutionism and Socialism or Communism'; 'traditional forms of peasant discontent' were 'virtually devoid of any explicit ideology, organization or programme'; 'pre-political people' are those 'who have not yet found, or only begun to find, a specific language in which to express their aspirations about the world' (pp. 5–6). His note cites 'Hobsbawm: 2, 5, 13, 23, 96, 118' and Hobsbawm and Rudé's Captain Swing (pp. 19, 205); his bibliography lists Primitive Rebels (Manchester, 1959) and Captain Swing (London, 1969). He grants the European case and notes an inconsistency: 'Hobsbawm's material is of course derived almost entirely from the European experience and his generalizations are perhaps in accord with it, although one detects a certain contradiction' between banditry having 'next to no organization or ideology' and being 'a rather primitive form of organized social protest' (p. 6). Then: 'Whatever its validity for other countries the notion of pre-political peasant insurgency helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India. For there was nothing in the militant movements of its rural masses that was not political' (p. 6). Elsewhere the book credits 'E. J. Hobsbawm's pioneering formulation of the concept of “social banditry”' (p. 90, read in the 1983 Delhi edition's text). Hobsbawm's words are given only as Guha quotes them; Primitive Rebels was not read. Guha's quotation has 'express their aspirations about the world', the wording the 1.132 review reported from an OCR witness of Primitive Rebels p. 2, where Chakrabarty (2000, Provincializing Europe p. 12) has 'express themselves'; Chakrabarty's Nepantla essay (2000, p. 16) also quotes 'aspirations', citing Hobsbawm (1978, 2). This gives a second, earlier quoted-in witness for the edge_917 wording question, not a reading of Hobsbawm. Reception: Chakrabarty credits the critique to Guha in Provincializing Europe (2000, p. 11; post source) and writes that rejecting the category 'fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity' (Nepantla, 2000, p. 19). No reply by Hobsbawm was looked for or read. This edge is the origin edge_917 (dipesh_chakrabarty → eric_hobsbawm) names ('the critique Guha began (1983)').

edges.relationship: Thompson's account of the rule of law as 'a cultural achievement of universal significance' (Whigs and Hunters, 1975) rejected from colonial India, where bourgeois culture 'hits its historical limit', after drawing on the same book for comparisons with peasant crime (1983–89)
edges.evidence_note: His own text. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography', Subaltern Studies VI (Delhi, 1989), pp. 276–277 read (Digital Library of India scan of the volume): asking 'What rule of law' existed under the Raj (p. 276), he finds the answer in 'the pervasive power of the ideology of law in English political thought', which assumed 'the status of “a cultural achievement of universal significance” in the eyes not only of English liberals and colonialists like Dodwell, but also, alas, of English radicals like E. P. Thompson from whom those words are taken' (p. 277). 'Neither the special pleading by Dodwell ... nor the ingenuity of Thompson when he tries unsuccessfully to disentangle himself from the metaphysical implications of his statement by allowing for the class manipulation of the rule of law, can take away from the fact that bourgeois culture hits its historical limit in colonialism' (p. 277). His notes cite Whigs and Hunters (London, 1975), p. 265, and pp. 258–69, especially 265–7. Whigs and Hunters was not read for this draft; the phrase is taken as Guha quotes it. The critique follows earlier use: Elementary Aspects (1983) draws on Thompson's account of the Blacks, the authorities' 'one common blur' of 'outrages by the Blacks' (p. 89) and the Blacks as an intermediate type between 'social bandits' and 'agrarian rebels' (p. 90), read in the 1983 Delhi edition's text. In-period context: Sarkar (1997, p. 83, read) writes that among historiographical influences on Subaltern Studies 'that of British Marxian social history was probably the most significant', that 'Ranajit Guha seems to have often used “subaltern” somewhat in the way Thompson deployed the term “plebeian”', and (n. 3) that Elementary Aspects 'frequently cited Thompson with approval', to Whigs and Hunters and Albion's Fatal Tree. The edge therefore records a dispute over one claim, not a rejection of Thompson. No reply by Thompson was looked for. edge_083 (marx → subaltern, Thompson's reception) stays.

edges.relationship: Gramsci's notes on subaltern groups, spontaneity and the 'first elements' of politics frame the founding preface and Elementary Aspects (1982–83); hegemony is later redefined against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony' (1989)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Preface to Subaltern Studies I (1982; Selected Subaltern Studies reprint, p. 35, read): the series cannot 'even remotely match the six-point project envisaged by Antonio Gramsci in his “Notes on Italian History”'; subordination is 'one of the constitutive terms in a binary relationship of which the other is dominance, for “subaltern groups are always subject to the activity of ruling groups, even when they rebel and rise up”'. The quoted words are Gramsci's (Selections from the Prison Notebooks, 1971, p. 55, checked in the gramsci source; the preface does not name the source). Elementary Aspects (1983), introduction read: the critique of 'pure spontaneity' follows 'Antonio Gramsci whose words are quoted above' ('there is no room for pure spontaneity in history', p. 5), with the quoted passage on a 'scholastic and academic historico-political outlook' (p. 4) taken from 'Spontaneity and Conscious Leadership' (n., Gramsci: 196–200); leadership is described 'in Gramsci's words, as “multiple elements of 'conscious leadership' but no one of them ... predominant”' (p. 10); and the book's title concept comes from the 'first elements' which Gramsci called 'the pillars of politics and of any collective action whatsoever' (p. 12, citing Gramsci: 144; the passage, 'Elements of Politics', checked at Selections p. 144). 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989, pp. 231–232, read): 'As used in this essay, hegemony stands for a condition of Dominance (D), such that, in the organic composition of the latter, Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)'; this 'avoids the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony (a term sometimes used in the Prison Notebooks synonymously with leadership) as antinomies, which has, alas, provided too often a theoretical pretext for the fabrication of a liberal absurdity—the absurdity of the idea of an uncoercive state—in spite of the basic drive of Gramsci's own work to the contrary'. The same definition is quoted from the 1997 book, p. 23, in Spivak's 'The New Subaltern' (Verso, 2000, n. 3), a later quoted-in witness. In-period readings: Sarkar (1997, p. 82) notes 'evocations of Gramsci' in Guha's 1982 preface and essay; O'Hanlon (1988; Verso reprint p. 102) finds 'no concerted attempt to construct a theory of domination as hegemony, as the invocation of Gramsci might have led us to expect', and agrees with Suneet Chopra and Javeed Alam 'that the series has not turned out to be a Gramscian project at all' (Alam and Chopra unread). Wikidata Q475026 states 'influenced by' Antonio Gramsci (P737); this is recorded as a Wikidata statement, not evidence. edge_159 (gramsci → subaltern) stays for the collective adaptation (for example David Arnold's 'Gramsci and Peasant Subalternity in India', reprinted in Mapping Subaltern Studies, 2000, ch. 3; not read); edge_159's evidence note names Guha, and a reviewer may trim that clause.

edges.relationship: Guha's critique of the 'pre-political' and his founding statements for Subaltern Studies, which Chakrabarty names as the starting point of his own argument for provincializing Europe (1997–2000)
edges.evidence_note: In Chakrabarty's own in-period words. 'Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts' (Perspectives, AHA, November 1997; subaltern source, read for 1.132) calls Guha 'the founder of the group'. Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction (post source, read for 1.132): Subaltern Studies registered 'a deep sense of unease with the very idea of the “political”', 'Nowhere ... more visible than in Ranajit Guha's criticism of the British historian Eric Hobsbawm's category “prepolitical” in his 1983 book Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency' (p. 11); Guha's critique 'fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity' (p. 14); 'My argument for provincializing Europe follows directly from my involvement in this project' (p. 15). 'Subaltern Studies and Postcolonial Historiography', Nepantla 1:1 (2000), pp. 9–32, read in the Project MUSE PDF: he reads 'the work of the historian Ranajit Guha in the period when he acted as the founding editor', 'the founding texts of the project' (p. 11), to show 'a radical departure from English Marxist historiographical traditions' (p. 11); 'In rejecting the category “pre-political”, however, Guha insists on the specific differences in the histories of power in colonial India and in Europe. This gesture is radical in that it fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity and separates it from any universal history of capital' (p. 19). He also reads a 'tension between a familiar narrative of capital and a more radical understanding of it' within Elementary Aspects, which 'sometimes does speak within' a Marxist transition narrative of 'lingering feudalism' (p. 18). Earlier, documented working ties: Guha's 1982 statement thanks 'Dipesh Chakrabarty' among those who commented on an earlier version (Selected Subaltern Studies reprint, p. 37, n. 1), and the Elementary Aspects preface names him among the colleagues of the collective who read the final draft. Criticism of the trajectory: Sarkar (1997, pp. 84–85) calls the path Chakrabarty outlined 'debilitating in both academic and political terms' (recorded on edge_915). This is an influence edge, not a claim that Chakrabarty's argument is Guha's; the Nepantla essay is Chakrabarty's own account of the project.
edges.map_label: From Guha's critique of the 'pre-political' to provincializing Europe, 1983–2000

edges.relationship: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’: the two senses of representation, the epistemic violence of colonial law and knowledge, and the subaltern woman silenced between colonial and indigenous patriarchal discourse on sati (1985–99)
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988), read in the Williams and Chrisman reprint (pages of that reprint; its opening is abridged): ‘Some of the most radical criticism coming out of the West today is the result of an interested desire to conserve the subject of the West, or the West as Subject’ (p. 66). ‘Two senses of representation are being run together: representation as “speaking for”, as in politics, and representation as “re-presentation”, as in art or philosophy’; ‘representing them, the intellectuals represent themselves as transparent’ (p. 70); running vertreten and darstellen together ‘leads to an essentialist, utopian politics’ (p. 71). The codification of Hindu law is her ‘example of epistemic violence’ (pp. 76–77), and she asks whether, ‘inside and outside the circuit of the epistemic violence of imperialist law and education’, ‘can the subaltern speak?’ (p. 78). On sati she sets the sentence ‘White men are saving brown women from brown men’, which she says she ‘put together’ (p. 92), against ‘the Indian nativist argument’, ‘“The women actually wanted to die”’: ‘The two sentences go a long way to legitimize each other. One never encounters the testimony of the women’s voice-consciousness’ (p. 93). She qualifies: ‘Given that the abolition of sati was in itself admirable’ (p. 94); ‘Obviously I am not advocating the killing of widows’ (p. 97). ‘Between patriarchy and imperialism, subject-constitution and object-formation, the figure of the woman disappears ... into a violent shuttling’ (p. 102). She welcomes ‘all the information retrieval in these silenced areas’ in history and other disciplines, while warning that the assumed ‘consciousness or subject’ will ‘cohere with the work of imperialist subject-constitution’ (p. 90). The close: ‘The subaltern cannot speak. There is no virtue in global laundry lists with “woman” as a pious item. Representation has not withered away’ (reprint p. 104, OCR damaged, wording restored from the unpaginated 1988 text in Morris, 2010; 1988 p. 308 per Sunder Rajan in the same volume). She credits Lata Mani’s 1983 thesis on sati as ‘a brilliant account’ and ‘profited from discussion with Ms Mani’ (n. 65, p. 109). The 1999 revision (A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, ch. 3; read in Morris’s unpaginated reprint; CPR p. 308 per Sunder Rajan) says: ‘in the first version of this text, I wrote, in the accents of passionate lament: the subaltern cannot speak! It was an inadvisable remark’, and that Bhubaneswari Bhaduri ‘was not a “true” subaltern’. ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (Critical Inquiry, 1985, read pp. 243–245) opens: ‘It should not be possible to read nineteenth-century British literature without remembering that imperialism, understood as England’s social mission, was a crucial part of the cultural representation of England to the English’, and finds it ‘particularly unfortunate when the emergent perspective of feminist criticism reproduces the axioms of imperialism’ (p. 243). In-period readings by historians: Gyan Prakash, ‘Can the “Subaltern” Ride?’ (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint 2000, pp. 226–227, read): ‘as Spivak states starkly, the debate left no room for the woman’s enunciatory position’; ‘Spivak very correctly marks the silencing of the subaltern woman as the point at which the interpreter must acknowledge the limits of historical understanding’. Sumit Sarkar, ‘Orientalism Revisited’ (Oxford Literary Review, 1994; reprint p. 254, n. 14, read), criticising Mani’s Saidian assumptions, contrasts ‘the much more substantive discussion of pre-colonial and colonial discourses on sati in Spivak’. Contested in period: Terry Eagleton (LRB, 13 May 1999; web text, no page numbers, read) on A Critique of Postcolonial Reason: ‘too well-mannered, as well as too episodic’ to be the critique its title promises, ‘too deeply invested in feminism and post-colonialism to launch a full-scale socialist critique of these currents’, yet ‘this study boldly addresses the economic realities which too many post-colonial critics culturalise away’; he reports that she contrasts her own critique with Aijaz Ahmad’s ‘scorching assault’ in In Theory (1992; unread here). Benita Parry, ‘Problems in Current Theories of Colonial Discourse’, Oxford Literary Review 9 (1987), pp. 27–58, is the best-known in-period critique; it is closed access and unread, and no claim is made about its argument. A contribution, not a founding: the post entry already lists Said (1978) before her, and edge_107 (language → post) and edge_115 (subaltern → post) stay.

edges.relationship: A critique from within: the collective's recovery of subaltern consciousness read as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', Guha's 'full autonomy' questioned, and woman shown to be 'the neglected syntagm' of its accounts of insurgency (1985–88)
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. ‘Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography’, Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363, read in full: the group ‘offers a theory of change’, plotting change ‘as confrontations rather than transition’ (p. 330); its practice is ‘closer to deconstruction’ than its self-description (p. 332); ‘This is why I hope to align them with deconstruction’ (p. 336). ‘Reading the work of Subaltern Studies from within but against the grain’ (p. 341), she reads the project to retrieve subaltern consciousness ‘as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest’ (p. 342), which ‘would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness’ (p. 356). On gender: ‘The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women’, but ‘I think they overlook how important the concept-metaphor woman is to the functioning of their discourse’ (p. 356); ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357); ‘Male subaltern and historian are here united in the common assumption that the procreative sex is a species apart’ (p. 358); ‘woman is the neglected syntagm of the semiosis of subalternity of insurgency’ (p. 359); ‘if the question of female subaltern consciousness ... is a red herring, the question of subaltern consciousness as such must be judged a red herring as well’ (p. 360). She qualifies: ‘The making-visible of the figure of woman is perhaps not a task that the group should fairly be asked to perform’, but ‘a feminist historian of the subaltern must raise the question of woman as a structural rather than marginal issue’ (p. 361). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): of Guha’s ‘autonomous domain’, ‘I cannot entirely endorse this insistence on determinate vigor and full autonomy’ (p. 79); ‘the colonized subaltern subject is irretrievably heterogeneous’ (p. 79); ‘If, in the context of colonial production, the subaltern has no history and cannot speak, the subaltern as female is even more deeply in shadow’ (pp. 82–83). In-period readings from historians of the field: Rosalind O’Hanlon, ‘Recovering the Subject’ (Modern Asian Studies, 1988; Verso reprint, read), takes up her phrase (p. 80, citing SS IV p. 342) but warns ‘we should certainly hesitate before accepting Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s suggestion that the strategy of the Subaltern series “in claiming a positive subject-position for the subaltern might be re-inscribed as a strategy for our times”’ (p. 105, citing SS IV p. 345). Gyanendra Pandey, a member, reads the 1988 close as Gramsci’s point: ‘“The subaltern cannot speak,” writes Gayatri Spivak, making, I suggest, much the same point’ (Ethnos, 1995; reprint p. 285, read). Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that the 1988 essay ‘brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies’ and ‘may have provided a major impetus’ for the gender and voice themes of Subaltern Studies IX (1996). Her own later account (‘The New Subaltern’, 2000, read): ‘Except in the work of Susie Tharu ... Subaltern Studies is not informed by feminist theory as such’ (p. 325), and of 1985, ‘Subaltern Studies had no need of such apologetics. edges.relationship: Foucault's account of power criticised as blind to imperialism and the international division of labour, and for an intellectual who lets the oppressed 'speak for themselves' while remaining transparent; his analyses of disciplinary institutions kept as useful (1988)
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period text: ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint, read in full). She takes as her object ‘Intellectuals and power: a conversation between Michel Foucault and Gilles Deleuze’ (p. 66), whose participants ‘systematically ignore the question of ideology and their own implication in intellectual and economic history’ (p. 66). In her summary of the conversation, ‘the oppressed can know and speak for themselves’ (p. 74); she adds ‘to Said’s analysis the notion of the surreptitious subject of power and desire marked by the transparency of the intellectual’ (p. 75). ‘Foucault is a brilliant thinker of power-in-spacing, but the awareness of the topographical reinscription of imperialism does not inform his presuppositions’ (p. 85); ‘The clinic, the asylum, the prison, the university - all seem to be screen-allegories that foreclose a reading of the broader narratives of imperialism’ (p. 86). She keeps part of his work: ‘what remains useful in Foucault is the mechanics of disciplinarization and institutionalization, the constitution, as it were, of the colonizer’ (p. 90), and calls his model of localized resistance ‘an admirable program’ that, universalized, ‘accommodates unacknowledged privileging of the subject’ (p. 85). Foucault’s position is given only as she presents it, from the translated conversation and Power/Knowledge; no reply was looked for (he died in 1984). Reception: Eagleton (1999, read) groups Derrida and Foucault as thinkers who ‘veer between a cult of theoretical “madness” ... and a more restrained, reformist sort of politics’, a criticism of her allies, not a defence of Foucault. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) carries her name with Stoler’s; see the optional relabel. Said’s separate critique of Foucault is pe137_said_rel_04 (said draft); she cites Said’s criticism and extends it (p. 75).

edges.relationship: Derrida's deconstruction, which she translated and introduced (1976), used and tested as a method for reading colonial texts and subaltern historiography, without being celebrated 'as feminism as such' (1976–88)
edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period texts. Translator’s preface to Of Grammatology (1976; read at p. lxxvii of the 1997 corrected edition): ‘To locate the promising marginal text, to disclose the undecidable moment, to pry it loose with the positive lever of the signifier; to reverse the resident hierarchy, only to displace it; to dismantle in order to reconstitute what is always already inscribed. Deconstruction in a nutshell. But take away the assurance of the text’s authority, the critic’s control, and the primacy of meaning, and the possession of this formula does not guarantee much.’ Subaltern Studies IV (1985): ‘This is the greatest gift of deconstruction: to question the authority of the investigating subject without paralysing him, persistently transforming conditions of impossibility into possibility’ (p. 336). ‘Three Women’s Texts’ (1985) sets ‘the lessons of deconstruction’ aside for the essay, choosing to ‘strategically take shelter in an essentialism’ (p. 244). ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ (1988; Williams and Chrisman reprint): ‘Derrida is hard to read; his real object of investigation is classical philosophy. Yet he is less dangerous when understood than the first-world intellectual masquerading as the absent nonrepresenter who lets the oppressed speak for themselves’ (p. 87); reading ‘Of grammatology as a positive science’, she reads him as placing the ethnocentric constitution of the Other as ‘Not a general problem, but a European problem’, and ‘As a postcolonial intellectual, I am not troubled that he does not lead me ... to the specific path that such a critique makes necessary’ (p. 89); ‘I have attempted to use and go beyond Derridean deconstruction, which I do not celebrate as feminism as such’ (p. 104); ‘In a certain way, then, the critique of imperialism is deconstruction as such’ (n. 47, p. 108). In-period reception: Eagleton (1999, read) calls Derrida ‘a consecrated figure for this book, about whom hardly a breath of criticism seems permissible’. Prakash (1992; reprint pp. 224–225, read) quotes her definition of deconstruction as an ‘impossible “no” to a structure, which one critiques, yet inhabits intimately’. Later reading, labelled: Chatterjee (2010) recalls that in 1982 the subalternists ‘did not imagine that Jacques Derrida ... could have anything remotely to do with Indian peasants’. Wikidata’s ‘influenced by’ (P737) lists Paul de Man, not Derrida; that is a Wikidata statement, not evidence here. Her translation’s publication dates (first American edition 1976, corrected 1997) are already checked on derrida_grammatology_corrected. edge_025 (derrida → post) tells her story under the group entry; see the proposed relabel.

edges.relationship: Chakrabarty uses 'Spivak's subaltern' as an analogy for the subject whom university history's transition narrative can only represent, the 'Indian' history that 'cannot speak itself as “theory”' (1992)
edges.evidence_note: Chakrabarty’s in-period text. ‘Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History’, Representations 37 (1992), read (JSTOR copy; spacing restored): the antihistorical subject ‘cannot speak itself as “theory” within the knowledge procedures of the university even when these knowledge procedures acknowledge and “document” its existence. Much like Spivak’s “subaltern” (or the anthropologist’s peasant who can only have a quoted existence in a larger statement that belongs to the anthropologist alone), this subject can only be spoken for and spoken of by the transition narrative’ (p. 19, n. 52, citing ‘Can the Subaltern Speak?’ and her 1990 Socialist Review interview). He also borrows, ‘in Gayatri Spivak’s words’, ‘the feeling of community that belongs to national links and political organizations’ (p. 18, n. 48, citing the 1988 essay at p. 277; Williams and Chrisman reprint p. 72); she is among those thanked in the unnumbered first note (p. 23), and n. 43 (p. 25) credits her with an expression (‘personal communication’). Her side, in period: Subaltern Studies IV (1985) discusses his labour essays (pp. 331, 344) and sets them against the collective’s neglect of gender: ‘Analogous research into the figure of the “worker” is performed by Chakrabarty. No such luck for the “female”’ (p. 357). The influence is bounded: Chakrabarty’s provincializing argument ‘follows directly’ from his work in Subaltern Studies (2000, p. 15; on edge_914), and the guha draft proposes Guha → Chakrabarty for the critique of the ‘pre-political’. This edge records one acknowledged borrowing in the 1992 programmatic essay, not a genealogy.

edge_604.relationship: Chatterjee extends the Subaltern critique from nationalist historiography to nationalist thought as a 'derivative discourse' (1986)
edge_604.evidence_note: Guha's 1982 statement (read) opened the critique of elite historiography; his own critique is the separate edge from his person entry. This edge records the distinct extension to nationalist thought. Sarkar (1997, pp. 91–92, read), a former member, traces how Partha Chatterjee's Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986) carried the critique to the colonized intelligentsia's 'derivative discourses', and objects that 'A project that had started with a trenchant attack on elite nationalist historiography had now chosen as its hero the principal iconic figure of official Indian nationalism' (p. 92). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000, p. 25) writes that Chatterjee's book 'extended Guha's criticisms of nationalist historiography into a full-blown, brilliant critique of nationalist thought itself'. The arrow does not claim a denial of all national histories.

edge_357.relationship: Subaltern Studies essays treat peasant, tribal and worker action under colonial rule as politics with its own forms, and are criticised for overstating its autonomy (1982–88)
edge_357.evidence_note: Sarkar (1997, pp. 86–87, read against the page images) lists early work that explored 'popular or subaltern autonomy in action, consciousness and culture': Hardiman on the peasant nationalists of Gujarat, Pandey on Congress organization and peasant militancy, Amin on rumours of Gandhi, studies of 'tribal movements and cults' and of Bengal labour. Bayly (1988; Verso reprint pp. 116–126, read) finds the essays' empirical work strong but holds that 'their concern to emphasize peasant autonomy seems to have deflected them from moving towards a “total history”' (p. 121) and that 'Simply to stress that autonomy ... is not very helpful in any attempt to specify the nature of historical change' (p. 126). O'Hanlon (1988; reprint pp. 85–86) criticises the 'literal interpretation of subaltern autonomy' in several contributions (Henningham, Ramachandra Guha, Dasgupta) while setting Ranajit Guha's book apart (p. 85). Ranajit Guha's own argument is the separate edge from his person entry.

edge_114.relationship: Subaltern Studies modifies the historiography of anti-colonial nationalism through an emphasis on 'pressures from below' and popular initiative beyond elite leadership (1982–88)
edge_114.evidence_note: Sarkar (1997, p. 86, read against the page image): the group's publications 'helped to significantly modify the historiography of anticolonial nationalism through a common initial emphasis on “pressures from below”', citing Hardiman, Pandey and Amin; it had been argued 'with considerable justice by Guha and other contributors' that anti-colonial movements had been explained 'far too often' by economic pressures and mobilization from the top (p. 85). He also notes that the critique of nationalist leaders restraining mass initiative 'had been quite common in some kinds of Marxist writing, most notably in R. P. Dutt's India Today' (p. 86, n. 8). The challenge concerns elite nationalist historiography, not every liberation movement or anti-colonial history.

edge_389.relationship: Feminist critics press Subaltern Studies on women's place in its accounts of labour and community (Nair, 1990), and gender becomes a theme of the series (1996)
edge_389.evidence_note: Janaki Nair's 1990 review in International Labor and Working-Class History questions Chakrabarty's treatment of gender in Bengal labour (graph verification note; gender strand bengal_labor_gender; not re-read here). Spivak's own 1985–88 critique is the separate edge from her person entry (revision 1.137); this edge records Nair's 1990 criticism and the series' 1996 uptake. Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' 'brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies' and that Subaltern Studies IX (1996) made 'gender issues' a dominant theme, with Kamala Visweswaran's 'Small Speeches, Subaltern Gender' and Susie Tharu and Tejaswini Niranjana's 'Problems for a Contemporary Theory of Gender' (both unread). Spivak (2000, p. 325, read) names Tharu as the member whose work is informed by feminist theory. The arrow records criticism and its uptake within the series; it does not claim that the collective adopted a feminist programme.

edge_025.relationship: Prakash defends deconstruction for postcolonial historical writing against O'Hanlon and Washbrook's charge of a 'residual positivism' (1992)
edge_025.evidence_note: Gyan Prakash, 'Can the “Subaltern” Ride?' (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint, pp. 224–227, read), defends deconstruction for historical writing under the heading 'Deconstructive Criticism and Historical Writing', reading Derrida's Of Grammatology and 'White Mythology' and answering O'Hanlon and Washbrook, who, as he quotes them, charge it with a 'residual positivism' and, in his paraphrase, with treating the historian's intervention in the past as illegitimate (p. 225, citing their p. 198, 2000 reprint pagination). O'Hanlon and Washbrook's own text is known here only through its first page and notes (pe132_ohanlon_washbrook_1992) and through Prakash's quotations. Rosalind O'Hanlon (1988; reprint p. 80, read) reads the Subaltern series' recovery of the subject as a 'strategy' whose 'limitations have yet to receive any proper public discussion'. Spivak's own use is the separate derrida → Spivak edge.

rationale: Person entries go to thinkers whose frameworks students meet across fields (user, 2026-10-13). Said's Orientalism, Guha's subaltern programme and Spivak's question of subaltern speech are read across postcolonial history, Subaltern Studies, gender, labour and world history. Chakrabarty became a person entry in 1.132 with no incoming edges; Guha and Spivak supply them on read evidence. Each draft's NOTES.md records what was read in full, in part, through reviewers or reprints, and what was not read (among them Ahmad's In Theory, Parry 1987, Clifford 1980, Rule of Property and the 1997 Dominance without Hegemony). In-period critics are kept: al-'Azm and Lewis on Said, with Clifford (1980) recorded but unread and Ahmad known only as reported; O'Hanlon, Bayly, Sarkar and Spivak herself on Guha; O'Hanlon and Eagleton criticise Spivak, while Prakash and Sarkar credit her sati discussion, and Parry (1987) is recorded but unread. Dissertation evidence is metadata only and never in entry text.
